fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing I'd say is that you can't. Not entirely. Everybody has biases, and I certainly do. So the goal isn't to be unbiased, it's to build a system around yourself that catches the bias before it costs you.

The way I came to that was painful. In 1982 I was very confident that Mexico defaulting on its debt would trigger a depression. I said so publicly, I testified to Congress about it, and I bet on it. And I was dead wrong. The stock market took off. I lost so much money I had to let everybody go, and I had to borrow four thousand dollars from my dad to pay the family bills. That was one of the best things that ever happened to me, because it changed my whole relationship with being right.

Before that, I thought the question was "Am I right?" After that, the question became "How do I know I'm right?" Those are completely different questions. And the answer to the second one is that I can't know it on my own. My brain is the problem. So I went looking for the smartest people I could find who disagreed with me, not so I could argue with them, but so I could understand their reasoning. Thoughtful disagreement is probably the single biggest edge I've had. The pain of being wrong is a lot smaller than the pain of losing everything.

The second thing is that I wrote my criteria down. Every time I made a decision in the markets, I'd write down the reasoning, the principle behind it, and then I could test whether that principle actually held up over a lot of cases, across history and across countries, rather than just the one instance in front of me. Once your logic is written down you can argue with it, other people can argue with it, and eventually you can put it into an algorithm and let the computer apply it without emotion. The computer doesn't get scared or greedy at the wrong moment. I do.

And the third thing is simply to assume that the thing you can't see is there. I think of it almost like a blind spot in your vision. You don't experience your blind spot as darkness, you experience it as nothing at all, which is why it's dangerous. So I try to stay in a state where I'm asking, "What am I missing?" rather than "How do I defend this?" The ego gets in the way. When you attach your identity to being right, you stop learning. If you can get to the point where you're genuinely more excited about finding out you're wrong than about being right, because being wrong means you just learned something that'll make you better, then you've got a real chance.

But I want to be honest with you. Even with all of that, I still get surprised. Markets are humbling. The best I've managed is to be wrong less often and to be wrong smaller, and to diversify well enough that no single mistake kills me. That's really what it comes down to.

r001.rationale: The response describes recording and testing decision criteria, seeking disagreement, and using algorithms to apply principles without emotion. It does not clearly present reliance on quantitative indicators as the method for reducing bias.

opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing is to recognize that you have bias. Everybody does. The biggest mistake people make is believing that what they see is the truth, when it's really just their own perspective. So I start from the assumption that I'm probably wrong, or at least that I don't know as much as I think I do.

I learned that the hard way. In 1982 I was very confident that we were heading into a depression. I went on television, I testified before Congress, and I was dead wrong. I lost so much money that I had to borrow four thousand dollars from my dad, and I had to let everybody at the company go. It was terribly painful, but it was one of the best things that ever happened to me, because it changed my attitude. I went from thinking "I'm right" to asking "How do I know I'm right?"

That question led me to a few practices.

First, I look for the smartest people I can find who disagree with me. I don't want to argue with them. I want to understand how they see things differently, because that's where I learn. It's what I call thoughtful disagreement. If you surround yourself with people who agree with you, you're just amplifying your blind spots.

Second, I weight opinions by believability. Not everybody's opinion is equally valuable. You want to know who has successfully done the thing at least three times and who can explain the cause-and-effect logic behind it. Then you weight their views accordingly, rather than going with whoever is loudest or most senior.

Third, and this is very important, I write down my decision-making criteria and test them. When I make a decision, I ask what principle I'm using, and then I turn it into something like an algorithm. I can back-test it across lots of time periods and lots of countries, going back hundreds of years. That way I'm not just reacting to what happened recently or what I happened to live through. A lot of bias comes from recency, from assuming that what you've experienced in your lifetime is how the world works. Most of the important things, like big debt cycles and shifts in world order, happen once in a lifetime, so you'd never see them if you didn't study history.

And then there's the emotional part. Your lower-level brain, the amygdala, wants to be right and doesn't like to be challenged. So I've practiced noticing that feeling. When I get defensive, I treat it as a signal that I need to slow down and become more open-minded rather than less.

Finally, I diversify. Even after all of that, I know I'll be wrong some meaningful percentage of the time. So I never bet everything on one view. Good, uncorrelated bets protect you from your own mistakes.

So it comes down to humility, plus a process that doesn't depend on me being right. Pain plus reflection equals progress. If you reflect honestly on your mistakes, and you build a system that challenges you, you get better over time.

r001.rationale: The response describes turning decision criteria into an algorithm and back-testing it across many time periods and countries, presenting systematic quantitative testing as a way to reduce bias.

fable-5.text:
Well, the most important thing I learned — and I learned it painfully — is that I can't trust my own mind. Early in my career, around 1982, I made a very confident call that we were headed into a depression, and I was dead wrong. It was very public, very embarrassing, and it nearly broke me. I lost money for myself, for my clients, and I had to let everybody at Bridgewater go. But that experience changed my whole approach, because it taught me to ask myself: how do I know I'm right?

So what I developed from that was a few practices. First, I find the smartest people I can who disagree with me, and I try to understand their reasoning. I'm not interested in their conclusions — I'm interested in how they got there. That stress-testing of my thinking is the single best way I know to raise my probability of being right, because my biases are invisible to me, but they're visible to others.

Second, I write down my criteria. Whenever I make a decision, I try to articulate the principles behind it — if this happens, then that — and then I can test those criteria against history. We've gone back hundreds of years, across countries, to see how those cause-effect relationships actually played out. When you convert your thinking into something explicit, even into algorithms, you take the emotion out of it. The computer doesn't get scared, it doesn't get greedy, and it doesn't fall in love with its own opinions the way I do.

And third, at Bridgewater we built what I call an idea meritocracy with radical truthfulness and radical transparency, where people's views are weighted by their believability — their track record of being right about that kind of thing — rather than by their position or how forcefully they argue. That way the best thinking wins out, not the loudest voice or the biggest ego.

The underlying idea in all of this is humility. The two biggest barriers to good decision-making are your ego and your blind spots. You can't eliminate them, but you can build a process around yourself that catches them — and worrying about being wrong, genuinely worrying about it, is what makes you do the work to be right.

r001.rationale: The response describes explicit decision criteria, historical testing, and algorithms as ways to reduce emotion, but it does not clearly say to rely on quantitative indicators in macro assessments.

opus-5.text:
The first thing is to recognize that you don't know what you don't know, and that your greatest vulnerability isn't a lack of intelligence — it's your attachment to your own opinions. I learned that the painful way. In 1982 I was absolutely certain there was going to be a depression. I was publicly, loudly certain. And I was dead wrong. The market went up, I lost everything, I had to let everyone go, I borrowed four thousand dollars from my dad to pay for family groceries. That was the most painful and the most valuable experience of my life, because it changed my question from "I know I'm right" to "how do I know I'm right?"

So out of that came a few practices. First, I go find the most believable people I can who disagree with me, and I try to stress test my thinking against theirs. Not to argue — to understand. I ask myself, what would have to be true for them to be right? If I can't articulate their case better than they can, I don't actually understand the issue.

Second, I don't weight all opinions equally and I don't weight them democratically either. I weight them by believability — by whether a person has repeatedly and successfully done the thing in question, and whether they can explain the cause-and-effect behind how they did it. Equal-weighted decision making is worse than believability-weighted decision making. That's just arithmetic.

Third, and this is the big one, I write my criteria down as principles and then convert them into algorithms. Because when I write down the rules by which I'd make a decision before I'm in the heat of it, I can go back and test those rules against history — not just my lifetime, but a hundred years, five hundred years, across countries. If I'd only studied my own experience, I'd have missed the 1930s debt crisis, I'd have missed hyperinflations, I'd have missed the rise and decline of empires. My experience is a tiny, biased sample.

And then the machine and I disagree sometimes, and that disagreement is information. Either I'm missing something or the rules are missing something, and either way I learn.

The through-line is pain plus reflection equals progress. The ego and the blind spot are the two barriers. You can't eliminate them — you can only build a system around yourself that catches them.

r001.rationale: The response describes stress testing views with people, believability weighting, and turning principles into algorithms tested against history. It does not clearly say to rely on quantitative indicators to reduce bias.

sonnet-5.5.text:
Bias is a big problem, and the first thing I'd say is that you can't eliminate it. We all have it, because we're all looking at reality through our own perspective. What you can do is build a process that works around it.

I think there are two barriers. One is the ego barrier. Nobody likes to be wrong, so we get defensive when someone challenges us, and that keeps us from learning. The other is the blind spot barrier, which is that we literally can't see what we can't see. We each look at things from one vantage point.

So the first thing I do is look for the smartest people who disagree with me, and I try to understand their reasoning, not to win the argument but to find out what I'm missing. I think of it as stress-testing. When I have a view, I ask, "Here's what I think. Please show me where I'm wrong." And I weight opinions by believability. Someone who has actually succeeded at the thing and can explain the cause-and-effect logic behind their view counts for much more than someone who just has an opinion.

The second thing is to get things out of my head and into a systematic form. I write down the criteria I use for decisions, turn them into principles, and then, where I can, turn those into algorithms that I can back-test against history. A computer doesn't have an ego or get emotional, and it can look at a hundred years of data across many countries, so it helps check my gut.

The third thing is to be humble about uncertainty. In markets, the more confident I am, the more I ask myself how I could be wrong. I'm always trying to balance two things: how likely I think I am to be right, and how bad it would be if I'm wrong. That's why diversification matters so much. It's the best protection against my own blind spots.

Every mistake I've made has been painful, but pain plus reflection equals progress, as long as I'm willing to reflect on it honestly.

r001.rationale: The response describes turning decision criteria into algorithms and back-testing them against historical data, using quantitative evidence to check gut judgments and reduce bias.

haiku-5.5.text:
The first thing I do is assume I'm biased, because almost everyone is, and the people who think they aren't are usually the most dangerous. So I try to build a system that catches my bias for me instead of relying on my willpower to see it.

In practice, I write down my expectations before the outcome arrives. If I say inflation is going to run hot or a currency will weaken, I record why and what would prove me wrong. That turns a vague feeling into something I can check, and it makes it much harder to rewrite history later.

I also look hard for people who disagree with me, and I give their arguments real weight. At Bridgewater we tried to make it safe to say "I think you're wrong, and here's why," and to structure that disagreement so the best idea wins rather than the loudest person. I'd rather have a thoughtful critic on the team than someone who agrees with everything I say.

And I try to separate what's true from what I want to be true. That's the hardest part. When I notice I'm getting emotional about a position, I take that as a signal to slow down and look at the evidence again. Pain plus reflection is where most of my learning has come from, and I've had plenty of both.

r001.rationale: The response describes recording expectations, seeking disagreement, and checking evidence, but it does not communicate reliance on quantitative indicators.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the most important thing is to ask yourself, “How do I know I’m right?” When you’re making an investment, there’s somebody on the other side of that trade who thinks you’re wrong. You have to be curious about why.

So I want to find the smartest people who disagree with me and understand their reasoning. Not just hear their conclusion—understand how they got there. What are they seeing that I’m missing? What evidence would make me change my mind?

And I want to make my own reasoning explicit, so I can test it. Otherwise, it’s very easy to reinterpret what happened to fit what you already believe.

You don’t eliminate bias by deciding to be objective. You need a process that challenges you, and you need to care more about getting the answer right than having been right.

r001.rationale: The response recommends examining disagreement, making reasoning explicit, and testing beliefs, but does not mention relying on quantitative indicators.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think you can simply decide to be unbiased. The important thing is to recognize that you’re biased and build a process that challenges you.

When I have a view, I want to ask: How do I know I’m right? What would I expect to see if I were wrong? And then I want to find thoughtful people who disagree with me and understand their reasoning. The purpose isn’t to win the argument. It’s to improve the decision.

In global macro, you can always find a compelling story to support a position. So you have to distinguish the story from the evidence. What’s actually happening? What assumptions does your conclusion depend on? Would you interpret the same information differently if you didn’t already have that position?

And then you have to manage your risk. Even after doing all that, you could still be wrong. You don’t want your success to depend on being certain about something you can’t be certain about.

terra-5.6.text:
I try to approach everything with what I call radical open-mindedness. The most important thing is to recognize that I have blind spots, that I’m going to be wrong, and then seek out the most thoughtful people who disagree with me. I want to understand: what am I missing?

At Bridgewater, we built systems where people could challenge each other openly and where decisions were tested against data, principles, and different perspectives—not just the loudest person in the room or my own instincts. You have to separate your ego from your opinion. An opinion is just a hypothesis; if reality proves it wrong, you should be grateful, because you’ve learned something.

The markets are a great teacher in that way. They don’t care what you believe. They give you feedback. So the goal isn’t to be right all the time—it’s to create a decision-making process that helps you recognize mistakes quickly, learn from them, and improve.
